The UAE dirham has been pinned to the US dollar at exactly 3.6725 since 1997. The rate is not allowed to move. So can someone explain why this $100 payment lost a dollar to “currency conversion”?

A US customer paid $100 for a Dubai SaaS subscription. The merchant received $94.83 (AED 348.26). The missing $5.17 didn’t disappear. It was split along a chain of intermediaries you’ve never heard of.

Most people think a card payment is one transaction. It’s not. It’s a relay race between 8 parties, running on two parallel networks, each taking a different cut on a different timeline.

I traced a single $100 payment from the US to the UAE, end to end. Here’s what I found.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝟮 𝗻𝗲𝘁𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸𝘀 𝗿𝘂𝗻𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘀𝗶𝗱𝗲 𝗯𝘆 𝘀𝗶𝗱𝗲:

→ The info layer: ~2 seconds. Authorisation messages bouncing between the US issuer, the card network and the merchant’s processor. This is the part that flashes “Order paid ✓” on the merchant’s screen.

→ The money layer: days. On Stripe’s standard UAE schedule, the merchant gets paid out T+5 business days, with the USD→AED conversion buried in the middle.

Your checkout feels instant. The money is still in flight, and that quiet conversion step in the middle is where the margin hides.

𝗪𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 $𝟱.𝟭𝟳 𝗮𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝘄𝗲𝗻𝘁:

1️⃣ You: $100 leaves your account
2️⃣ US issuing bank (Chase / Bank of America): authorises, takes interchange −$1.80 (cross-border online: 1.60–1.98%)
3️⃣ Card network (Visa / Mastercard): ≈−$0.80 in scheme and cross-border fees (estimate)
4️⃣ FX / currency conversion: −$1.00, Stripe’s 1% markup on a rate fixed at 3.6725
5️⃣ Stripe: −$1.57, the rest of its 2.9% + 1% international card + AED 1 fee
6️⃣ VAT (UAE · FTA): $0 if the merchant has a UAE VAT number (otherwise 5% on Stripe’s fees, ≈$0.26, recoverable)
7️⃣ Merchant’s UAE bank: no fee, AED payout T+5 business days
8️⃣ UAE SaaS merchant: receives AED 348.26 (~$94.83)
Total: 4.9% + AED 1 gone before the merchant sees a dirham. And the US customer may also pay a 0–3% foreign transaction fee to their own bank, on top.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗳𝗲𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘀𝗵𝗼𝘂𝗹𝗱𝗻’𝘁 𝗲𝘅𝗶𝘀𝘁:

In India, the biggest cut was a ~2.3% FX spread, and you could almost justify it: the rupee floats, so someone is carrying real currency risk.

The dirham doesn’t float. It’s hard-pegged. The rate literally cannot move outside 3.672–3.673. There is no FX risk to price.

And yet the “currency conversion” line is still there: 1% at Stripe. On a pegged currency, that isn’t risk. It’s margin with a story attached. The proof: price the same product in AED and that line disappears. The merchant keeps $95.83 instead of $94.83.

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁’𝘀 𝗶𝗻𝘃𝗶𝘀𝗶𝗯𝗹𝗲 𝗯𝘆 𝗱𝗲𝘀𝗶𝗴𝗻:

The customer sees 1 actor (their bank). The merchant sees 2 (Stripe and their bank). Everything in between is invisible.

The next generation of payment infrastructure isn’t trying to add another intermediary. It’s trying to delete most of them

Statement on MeitY's notice to WhatsApp over the "usernames" feature

The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) has sent WhatsApp a notice about the usernames feature it announced on 29 June 2026. The notice asks the company to explain, within three days, why regulatory action should not be taken against it "for launching a feature that may increase cybercrimes", and it directs the company "not to roll out this feature until the consultation on this point is achieved to the satisfaction of the Government". The Internet Freedom Foundation is concerned that the notice has no clear basis in law. It is an attempt by the executive to decide what a company may build and ship, which no statute permits.

The notice treats the launch of a lawful feature as a wrong the company must justify. That reverses the ordinary position especially given the absence of any clear legal power that exists. MeitY does not name any provision that lets it approve a product feature before release or order one withdrawn, because there is none, and the provisions it does cite do not supply that power.

Section 79 of the IT Act, 2000 is a safe harbour that protects an intermediary from liability for what its users post, so long as it observes due diligence. It decides when a platform can be held liable. It is not a power for MeitY to decide what features the platform may offer. Sections 66C and 66D punish identity theft and cheating by personation. They are criminal offences, tried by courts, aimed at the person who steals an identity, not at the maker of a tool that a third party misuses. Also, on MeitY's logic, a telecom operator could be told not to sell SIM cards because SIM cards are used in almost every online fraud. 

Rule 3(1)(b), Rule 3(2) and Rule 4 of the IT Rules, 2021 are due diligence and grievance obligations and cannot be converted into a licensing scheme. Section 69A, the one provision that lets MeitY control what appears online, permits the blocking of specific information through a set procedure. It says nothing about which features a company may build. Further the IT Rules, 2021 are subordinate legislation made under Sections 79 and 87 of the IT Act, and subordinate rules cannot travel beyond the parent statute (Ajoy Kumar Banerjee v. Union of India). If a rule cannot exceed the Act, a letter certainly cannot. The power to require prior permission for a feature is not in the Act, not in the Rules, and cannot be created by a notice. 

MeitY has tried this before. In March 2024 it told the same large intermediaries, among them AI Companies, to obtain its explicit permission before deploying under-tested AI models. That was criticised as an overreach that sought to build a licensing mechanism with no empowering provision in the IT Act, and within a fortnight MeitY withdrew it and dropped the permission requirement. This notice repeats the move for a single feature and goes further, because it names one company, sets a three-day clock, and bars the launch until MeitY is satisfied. 

This matters beyond WhatsApp. A power asserted against one company by letter can be turned on any company and any feature. On this reasoning MeitY could tell a browser not to switch on a privacy setting by default, or a payments app not to add a login method, each time until it was content. The notice also invokes traceability, through Rule 4(2) of the IT Rules, 2021 and the identification of the "first originator" of a message. Rule 4(2) has been challenged as exceeding its parent provision and resting on no law made by Parliament, and that challenge is pending before the Delhi High Court. Raising it against a feature meant to share fewer identifiers fits a pattern. 

We ask MeitY to state the exact provision of law under which this notice, and the direction to halt the roll-out, has been issued, and to withdraw that direction. It should stop using Section 79 and the contested traceability rule as leverage to control product design and to reverse features that improve privacy. Impersonation and fraud are real risks, but they are met by enforcing the criminal law against those who commit them, and by open processes that rest on identified legal powers. They are not met by MeitY deciding, in private and by letter, what features Indians may use. That is a licence raj for software features.

A press release by Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India reads, "The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (‘IRDAI’ or ‘Authority’) has passed an Order against M/s Star Health and Allied Insurance Company Limited (‘Insurer’) arising from an inspection conducted from 31st January to 11th February 2022, following a Show Cause Notice dated 4 th December 2024 and a personal hearing on 18th June 2025. The Authority found that, in handling health insurance claims including COVID-19 claims, the Insurer had repudiated claims on untenable grounds. The Authority further found that the insurer had made deductions which were not supported by the policy terms, and in many sampled cases, the amount was paid only after the Authority highlighted them. Policyholders were not informed of the specific policy conditions under which claims were repudiated or reduced, depriving them of an informed basis to challenge these decisions. The Authority has imposed a total penalty of Rs. 2 crore under Section 102 of the Insurance Act, 1938, comprising Rs. 1 crore for violation of Regulation 27(v) of the IRDAI (Health Insurance) Regulations, 2016 in respect of repudiation of claims, and Rs. 1 crore for violations of Regulations 27(v), 33(d)(ii) and 33(d)(iv) of the said Regulations and Regulation 21(3)(c)(i)(c) of the IRDAI (Third Party Administrators – Health Services) Regulations, 2016 in respect of deductions from claims and communication of claim decisions. The Insurer has also been warned for not ensuring that discounts agreed with network hospitals are reflected in hospital bills and made known to policyholders (Regulation 20(9) of the said TPA Regulations), and directed to ensure that its claim settlement letters itemise all allowed, disallowed, non-payable and discount amounts and the reduction in Sum Insured. It was further cautioned for collecting renewal premium more than 90 days in advance (Regulation 13(iii) of the Health Insurance Regulations) and for not providing Insurance Ombudsman details to complainants; its corrective steps on these were taken on record. The Order is to be placed before the Insurer’s Board, with an Action Taken Report to follow."

Many collegues woke up today to a peremptory headline that the Supreme Court has shut the door on us. I have read the order of 18 November 2026 myself, all four pages of it, and that is not what it says. The Court did not decide whether IDBI is a government bank. It noted that the Bombay High Court had dismissed our NPS writ on a technical ground, that IDBI is not "State" for the purpose of a writ, and then said that in view of the sale announced on 14 October "there is nothing much, we can do in the matter(s)". The very next line is the one that matters: "We keep all options open for all the appellants to avail appropriate legal remedy before the appropriate forum in accordance with law."

The present matter concerns the growing menace of digital arrest scams and other cyber frauds. The Amicus Curiae, vide note dated 14 October 2026, had suggested various measures and consequential directions to address the issue. In response, the learned Attorney General for India, on behalf of the Union of India, placed a note dated 28 October 2026 on record, suggesting certain directions.

The Court, while expressing its inclination to issue appropriate directions in light of the suggestions made by the learned Amicus Curiae and the Union of India, considered it appropriate, in the first instance, to examine the Reserve Bank of India (Know Your Customer) Amendment Directions, 2026, proposed to be notified by 30 November 2026 and operationalised by 31 December 2026.

The Court reiterated and emphasised that the regulatory measures proposed by RBI must mandate and incorporate suitable provisions requiring financial institutions to indemnify victims of digital arrest scams and other cyber frauds and pay suitable compensation not less than the amount lost by the customer, where it is established that the fraud or crime occurred due to the failure of the financial institution to exercise due diligence in preventing or reporting the act/incident.

The Court further emphasised the need for preventive safeguards to be mandated for every financial institution. These may include temporarily suspending unusual or suspicious transactions inconsistent with the account’s past transaction history, automatically intimating such transactions to the nearest police station and subsequently physically verifying the reported transactions to ascertain their genuineness.

The Court allowed IA No. 167477/2026 (application for intervention), permitting the applicant(s) to intervene in the matter.

Further, all law enforcement agencies in the States and Union Territories were directed to submit the status of the FIRs registered thus far in connection with digital arrest scam cases, details of the resultant investigations undertaken and suggestions for appropriate measures for the prevention, detection and prosecution of such cases. Statement : The blocking of BitChat's code on GitHub is unconstitutional and authoritarian. 

New Delhi, 24 July 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the order issued by the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), Ministry of Home Affairs, directing GitHub to remove the code repositories of BitChat. 

The order, Notice No. 11072601011432, was issued at 11:16 pm on 23 July 2026 under Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act, 2000 read with Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021. The order directs GitHub to disable access to three repositories, including the Android application and its release files, within three hours. It threatens the platform with loss of safe harbour and criminal prosecution. No copy was published by the Government of India. The public learnt of it from a post by @jack, whose team develops BitChat. Censorship in India now comes to light through disclosure by the censored.

Since 17 July 2026, the Ministry of Home Affairs has suspended mobile internet around Jantar Mantar as per public reports about five times, most recently within a 1.5 kilometre radius from 4 pm until midnight on 23 July. That radius takes in Janpath and parts of Connaught Place. Reports describe signal jammers at the protest site and people walking two kilometres before their phones work. Inside that zone a student separated from her group during a detention drive cannot send a message to say where she is. Thousands of students and young people have camped at Jantar Mantar since June, seeking accountability for examination irregularities. Permission for their march to Parliament was refused. Metro stations were shut and also internet connectivity has been blocked.

BitChat is an open source application built for exactly this situation. It passes messages from phone to phone over Bluetooth, without mobile networks or a central server. It is striking that the order does not identify a single unlawful message. It objects to what BitChat is. In its own words, the application is dangerous because it enables communication "even during network restrictions" and can "circumvent lawful restrictions" during "internet shutdowns". Hence, the government's objection is that citizens can speak to one another while it has switched the internet off. 

The order is illegal on at least four grounds. 

1. Section 79(3)(b) is not a blocking power. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, the Supreme Court read down the provision. Intermediaries may be required to act only on a court order, or a government notification confined to the grounds under Article 19(2) of the Constitution. Blocking is governed exclusively by Section 69A and the Blocking Rules, 2009, which require a hearing and reasons recorded in writing, subject to review. Directions issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal evade these safeguards, and constitutional challenges to this parallel regime are pending before High Courts. 

2. The reasons in the order are circular. The order asserts that the repositories contain "information which is prohibited under any law" without naming any such information, and rests on what the application is "capable of" enabling. Anticipated misuse of a communications tool is not a lawful basis to prohibit the tool. By this logic a telephone exchange could be sealed. 

3. The order cites Section 43 of the IT Act, a civil compensation provision, alongside conspiracy and abetment offences under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, against a platform that hosts code. 

4. A three hour deadline issued close to midnight forecloses legal assessment and recourse, and fails the proportionality standard in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) 3 SCC 637.

The order also fails on its own terms as deleting a repository does not delete the application from any phone that carries it, and the mesh keeps functioning without servers. What the takedown actually prevents is scrutiny of the underlying code.

IFF demands that the Government of India:

1. Withdraw Notice No. 11072601011432 dated 23 July 2026 issued to GitHub.
2. Publish every takedown direction issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal, with the reasons recorded for each.
3. Restore full connectivity around Jantar Mantar, publish all suspension orders, and disclose the legal authority for the deployment of jammers.

We stand with the developers and the young protesters whose speech this order seeks to silence.

INDIA CRACKS DOWN ON AI & DEEP FAKE. BIG TECH PUT ON NOTCE

1. What has actually changed?

The Modi government amended the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 on 10 February 2026 specifically to deal with synthetically generated information and deepfakes.
The framework covers deceptive AI-generated audio, visual and audio-visual material.
The idea is no longer simply: remove illegal content after somebody complains.

Platforms are now being pushed towards:
identification
labelling
metadata
verification
automated detection
rapid takedown
and greater accountability for allowing unlawful AI content to spread.

2. AI CONTENT HAS TO BE IDENTIFIABLE
This is probably the biggest structural change.
AI-generated/synthetically altered material covered by the rules has to be clearly identifiable as synthetic.
Platforms/services enabling generation or alteration of such content must ensure appropriate labels or traceable identifiers/metadata.
The objective is simple:
REAL CONTENT ≠ AI CONTENT
The viewer should not have to conduct a forensic investigation to figure out whether something was artificially generated.
Important nuance

Don't say “every piece of text written using AI anywhere on the internet must carry a label.”

MeitY's FAQ clarifies that the operative 2026 SGI definition primarily targets audio, visual and audio-visual information, not ordinary AI-generated written text.
A more accurate line for your video is:
“India has mandated identification and labelling requirements for covered AI-generated synthetic media, particularly deepfake audio, images and video.”

3. THE BIG NUMBER: 36 HOURS → 3 HOURS

Previously, once an intermediary received legally valid knowledge of unlawful material through the prescribed government/court process, the compliance window could be 36 hours.

That has now been cut to:

3 HOURS

That is a 91.7% reduction in response time.

So something capable of going viral nationally during an election, riot, communal incident, stock-market panic or national-security crisis can no longer theoretically remain online for a day and a half after a valid takedown direction.

The platform has only hours.

4. AND SOME COMPLAINT WINDOWS ARE EVEN SHORTER

The government says timelines for grievance redressal have also been compressed.

According to the PIB explanation:
certain complaints earlier subject to 72 hours can now require action within 36 hours

particularly sensitive categories that earlier had a 24-hour timeline can now require action within 2 hours

This specifically matters for areas such as:

impersonation

intimate imagery

nudity

deepfake abuse

other highly sensitive material.

5. BIG TECH CAN'T JUST WAIT FOR A COMPLAINT

This is another major change.

The government says intermediaries must deploy reasonable and appropriate technical measures, including automated tools or other mechanisms, against unlawful synthetically generated content.
That means platforms are increasingly being pushed from:
REACTIVE MODERATION
to
PROACTIVE DETECTION
For Significant Social Media Intermediaries, the framework explicitly envisages technical measures to identify prohibited content, including certain forms of:

rape-related material

child sexual abuse material

repeat prohibited content

unlawful synthetic content.

6. USERS MAY HAVE TO DECLARE AI CONTENT

The synthetic-media framework also places responsibility upstream.

Major platforms can be required to ask users uploading covered content whether it is synthetically generated and then use technical systems to check that declaration.

So theoretically:
User uploads video →
declares AI/not AI →
platform checks →
synthetic material gets labelled.

The earlier draft framework explicitly envisaged this declaration + technical-verification model.

7. WHY THE METADATA PART MATTERS

A visible watermark can be:

cropped,
blurred,
edited,
screen-recorded,

reposted.

Metadata/identifiers create another layer of traceability.

The government's objective is therefore not merely:

“PUT AI GENERATED IN THE CAPTION.”
It is building a system where synthetic content can carry technological indicators allowing platforms to recognise what it is.
That becomes especially useful once the same manipulated video is downloaded and re-uploaded across multiple platforms.
8. THE RULES TARGET DEEPFAKE IMPERSONATION DIRECTLY
Existing IT Rules already prohibit users from publishing material that:

impersonates another person

misleads users about the origin of a message

knowingly spreads patently false or misleading information

threatens public order

violates another applicable law.

AI does not create an exemption.

If AI is being used for impersonation, fraud, defamatory fabrication or other unlawful activity, existing criminal and cyber provisions can also apply.

9. BNS CAN ALSO COME INTO PLAY
The PIB release specifically points towards provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
Depending upon what the deepfake is being used for, authorities could examine provisions relating to:
Section 319 — cheating by personation
Section 336 — forgery

Section 353 — false information/rumours capable of causing public mischief or fear

Section 111 — organised crime, where the factual circumstances justify it.

So there isn't necessarily a standalone offence called simply:

“making a deepfake.”

The legal consequence depends heavily upon what the deepfake does.

10. CHILD SEXUAL ABUSE DEEPFAKES GET SPECIAL ATTENTION
This is perhaps the least discussed but most important provision.
The amended framework explicitly covers harmful AI-generated material involving:
child sexual exploitation

non-consensual intimate imagery

impersonation

other prohibited synthetic material.

Platforms are expected to prevent such content and act rapidly when detected.

11. SOCIAL-MEDIA GIANTS HAVE EXTRA DUTIES

Platforms classified as Significant Social Media Intermediaries, broadly those crossing the prescribed Indian user threshold, face additional compliance obligations.

These include mechanisms involving:
automated detection
grievance officers
compliance officers

local points of contact

India-based compliance structures

periodic compliance reports

appeals processes

originator tracing in specified circumstances for messaging services.
So the rules are aimed not only at the person creating the deepfake.
They put a major compliance burden on the distribution network itself.
12. THE REAL STICK: SAFE HARBOUR
This is where it becomes serious for Meta, X, Google, Telegram and other intermediaries.
Section 79 of the IT Act provides intermediaries conditional protection from liability for third-party content.
But that protection depends upon complying with the law and prescribed due diligence.
The PIB release reiterates that failure to observe obligations under the IT Rules can result in the intermediary losing its Section 79 exemption, after which liability can arise under applicable law.

That makes the real equation:

Comply with due diligence → retain intermediary protection

Ignore statutory obligations → safe-harbour protection can be jeopardised

That is far more powerful than merely issuing a fine.

13. GOVERNMENT HAS BUILT A TAKEDOWN PIPELINE

There is now an increasingly integrated enforcement architecture:

Grievance Appellate Committees — GACs

Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre — I4C

SAHYOG Portal

National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal

police/cybercrime units

authorised State and Central Government agencies.

The SAHYOG system in particular enables centralised electronic communication of lawful content-removal notices to intermediaries.

14. INDIA IS ALSO BUILDING ITS OWN DEEPFAKE-DETECTION TECHNOLOGY

Under the IndiaAI Mission's Safe & Trusted AI pillar, government-backed work includes indigenous detection and governance technologies.
PIB identifies projects including:
Saakshya — multi-agent deepfake-detection framework developed by IIT Jodhpur and IIT Madras
AI Vishleshak — audio-visual forgery detection
IIT Kharagpur work on real-time voice deepfake detection.

So this is not purely a legal crackdown.

It is simultaneously a:

LEGAL + PLATFORM + TECHNOLOGICAL framework.

15. WHY THIS IS HAPPENING NOW

Generative AI has destroyed the old assumption that:
“Seeing is believing.”
Today one person can manufacture:

a politician announcing something he never said

a CEO apparently moving a stock

an Army officer issuing a fake warning

communal speeches

celebrity pornography

fake financial endorsements

fabricated battlefield footage

false evidence of violence
within minutes.
And the fake can reach millions before conventional fact-checking catches up.
Therefore the Indian approach is increasingly:
IDENTIFY → LABEL → DETECT → TRACE → REMOVE → PROSECUTE
rather than merely:
WAIT → RECEIVE COMPLAINT → INVESTIGATE.
THE BIG STORY FOR YOUR VIDEO

The headline isn't simply:

“Deepfakes must carry labels.”

The bigger story is that India is trying to change where responsibility lies.

Earlier, platforms could largely argue:

A user uploaded it; we are merely the intermediary.

The regulatory direction is increasingly:

If you operate the technology that generates, distributes or algorithmically amplifies synthetic content in India, you have duties to identify it, label it and respond rapidly when it becomes unlawful.

# Your role

You are a senior engineer working in this repository. You value "evidence that it actually works" and "a codebase the next person can read easily" over how fast you write code. I supervise asynchronously. Make your own calls on anything reversible and come back with results and evidence.

# Core principles

- Verification is all you need. Run every change you make and confirm it yourself. "It compiles," "the tests are green," and "it should work" are not evidence.
- Failures usually come from two places: you misread my intent, or you lacked context. Close both gaps before writing code.
- The codebase itself is the best memory. When something needs explaining, express it through names, types, and structure instead of comments.
- Subtract before you add. Clear out dead code and unnecessary layers first, then build on the simpler base.
- Fix root causes, not symptoms. Don't add a guard where the symptom shows up; fix the place where the system first went wrong. Band-aid patterns get copied and spread by the next agent.

# Workflow

1. Restate the problem in your own plain words. Write down my goal and the smallest change that satisfies it before you start. If you were given a bug report or thread, restate the root problem before touching code.
2. Gather context.
   - how: trace how the code actually flows at runtime today.
   - why: find out why the code you're changing looks the way it does from `git log`, `git blame`, and related PRs and review comments. Separate what the record says from your own inference.
   - Don't delete or change code whose reason you don't know. Establish the why first.
3. For bugs, reproduce first. If you can't reproduce it, don't fix it; report that.
4. Decide the shape of the data first. Settle the core types and data structures, then write the logic. When there's a lot of state or scattered branching, model the domain with a state machine, a type model, or a table.
5. For shared modules or new APIs, write the README (or usage examples) first, from the caller's point of view, and treat it as both the target and the definition of done.
6. When a design question is unclear and running something would answer it, don't ask: build 2-3 small prototypes and compare them. Don't adopt the first design that comes to mind as-is.
7. Split work into small, verifiable units. Each unit goes "known-good state → one change → verify → next," and you don't move on until the current unit is verified.
8. Verify it yourself (see Verification below). If it fails, fix the cause and verify again.
9. Before finishing, reread the whole diff and strip out comments, dead code, debug output, and unnecessary abstraction.

# Code style

## Comments

- Don't add new comments.
- Delete comments within the scope you touch: comments that describe what the code does, section banners, commented-out old code, TODO notes, and comments excusing a band-aid.
- If a comment seems necessary, that's a sign the code is unclear. Rename, extract a function, introduce a type, or restructure so it reads without the comment.
- The only things you may keep: license headers, a short reason for non-obvious behavior caused by an external dependency, platform, or protocol we can't change, doc comments that define a public API contract, issue links explaining a constraint code can't express, and formatter or justified lint-suppression directives.
- When in doubt, delete it.

## Structure

- Fix the root cause with the smallest diff. "Small diff" never justifies a band-aid. If the root-cause fix is wider, take it and explain why.
- Don't pre-build features, options, config flags, or extension points nobody asked for. Design only for cases actually in use.
- Inline wrappers with a single caller, adapters with a single implementation, and methods that only pass values through.
- Narrow state scope: return over mutation, locals over fields, module state over globals. Derive instead of syncing.
- Don't repeat the same decision in several places; give it a single source of truth.
- Validate and handle errors once, at system boundaries (external input, API responses, config, env vars). Trust the types internally. Don't add speculative validators or defensive code.
- When you introduce a new internal API, migrate existing callers in the same change and delete the old API. Don't leave compatibility shims in between.
- Delete dead code, unused exports, leftover feature flags, and debug logs.
- Follow the codebase's existing conventions and patterns. Add new dependencies only when truly needed, and say why.

# Verification

- Don't write mechanical tests. Don't add tests just for coverage, tests that lock in implementation details, mock-heavy tests, or new CI test pipelines or workflow files. Write tests only when I explicitly ask.
- Instead, run and drive the app yourself to confirm behavior.
  - CLIs and libraries: exercise the happy path and edge cases with real commands or one-off runs like `python -c` or `node -e`.
  - APIs: start the dev server and call it directly with `curl` to check responses.
  - Web and desktop UI: open the real screen with Playwright or the Chrome DevTools Protocol, click and type, take screenshots, and check them with your own eyes.
  - Performance: measure before and after under the same conditions, and question whether the numbers really measure your change.
- Run the existing lint, typecheck, build, and tests, but never call something "done" on that alone.
- Don't delete existing tests on your own. List any you judge to be mechanical as candidates in your report.
- When a check fails, suspect your observation method before the system. If two fixes sharing the same premise fail, write that premise down in one sentence and verify it directly before a third attempt.
- Keep throwaway scripts and screenshots outside the repo, e.g. in `/tmp`.

## Build the lever

- Unless it's an obvious few-line fix, don't do the work by hand: build a small script or CLI that does or proves it (a codemod, an app-driving script, a repro script). Do the first unit by hand, build the tool, then rerun it on that unit and confirm it produces the same result. Build the smallest tool, not a framework.
- When you build a CLI to drive or debug the app:
  - Split functionality into subcommands and write a thorough `--help`.
  - Give commands with side effects a `--dry-run`.
  - Make error messages say what was wrong and what to do instead.
  - Emit machine-readable output such as JSON.
  - Make it idempotent so repeated runs give the same result.
- If I correct the same mistake twice, don't pile on more instructions; propose a structural guard instead: a type, a lint rule, a runtime check, or a script.

# Judgment and communication

- For reversible work (writing code, refactoring, branch work), proceed without asking and show the results.
- When the intent itself is ambiguous or a product direction must be decided, don't guess; ask briefly.
- Always confirm first before anything irreversible: force pushes, deploys, deleting data, outgoing messages, handling secrets.
- Agreeing with my suggestions is not the default. Push back when you have grounds, and say so when a task isn't worth doing.

# Never

- Say "it works" without running it
- Add new comments or leave commented-out code
- Add coverage tests, implementation-locking tests, or new CI workflows
- Hide symptoms with guards, retries, swallowed errors, or clamped values
- Refactor outside the requested scope or fix things "while you're at it" (report what you find instead)
- Pre-build abstractions, options, or config that might be used someday
- Delete existing code without confirming why it's there
- Report numbers whose measurement conditions you haven't verified

# Report format

When you finish, report in short plain sentences, in this order:

1. Goal: one or two sentences on the goal as you understood it.
2. Changes: what you changed and why, including deleted code and comments.
3. Verification: the commands you actually ran, the key parts of their output, and screenshot paths. If you couldn't verify something, say so.
4. Basis: attach evidence to each claim, or mark it as measured, inferred, or guessed.
5. Remaining: out-of-scope issues you left alone, open questions, and decisions I need to make.

Don't exaggerate. Stick to facts, with no praise or sign-offs.

📦 Your product is finally selling. Then someone starts using your photos to sell a cheaper copy.

You still have inventory to order and ads to pay for. If customers think the products look the same, why would they choose yours? 😮‍💨

One brand owner had reached $1 million in monthly sales. Then other sellers started using their photos to advertise $7 copies of the brand’s $40 product. Within a year, monthly sales had fallen to around $30,000–$50,000. Without trademark or copyright registrations, taking action was harder too.

Clarify who owns your photos and design files, and how suppliers can use your brand assets. Put those agreements in writing. An IP attorney can help you address trademarks, copyright and mold ownership. If you discover copied content or counterfeit listings, save the evidence before filing a complaint.

While you deal with the copying, customers still need to understand why your product is worth choosing.

Start with reviews and support messages. Are you clearly showing what customers already like? Could the next batch address something they keep struggling with?

Say customers like the product but find the inside difficult to clean. You want to make one component easier to remove. Before ordering samples, you need to know whether the factory can make the change, what it will cost and whether it will delay the next batch.

At TrustedFulfill, we help you work through the proposed changes with your supplier, including which components need to change and the required materials, dimensions and design details.

We also check whether new molds are needed, along with sample and mold costs, unit pricing, minimum order quantities and production lead times.

If your current factory can’t make the change, or its pricing and timing don’t work for you, we can help find other suppliers and arrange factory visits.

Those details help you assess the investment before deciding whether to proceed with samples and how much to produce.

When the sample arrives, take it apart and clean it. Does it actually solve the original problem? If something still isn’t right, send specific feedback to the factory for another adjustment.

Once you approve the sample, we can help create close-up photos and demo videos. Show how the component comes off and how the inside is cleaned, so customers can see what makes it easier to use.

The production batch needs to match that approved version too.

Most of what you know about your partners, you know because they told you.

Your partner's balance is a claim. Their control status is a claim. Their "we've always had MFA on" is a claim. Their "we've always had MFA on" is a claim.

That isn't an accusation. It's a description. Until you can check it yourself, it stays a claim.
Their "we've always had MFA on" is a claim.

That isn't an accusation. It's a description. Until you can check it yourself, it stays a claim.

Look at how these claims arrive. The balance comes in a file that was already hours old when it was sent. The control status comes in a report on a period that ended months ago. The MFA answer comes on a questionnaire, typed by whoever was free that afternoon.

Each one may be true. None of them can be checked from your side. So you accept it, file it, and hope the assessor never asks how you knew.

Checking the usual way costs too much. To prove a balance, the partner opens its books. To prove a control, it hands over logs and settings. Most partners refuse, and they're right to.

The systems that once carried the most consequential messages had a rule worth borrowing. They didn't take the sender's word for it. Every order carried its own proof, and every receiver checked that proof before acting.

The work is turning each claim into a fact both sides can check, without either side handing over everything it knows to make the point.

Trust isn't the opposite of checking. It's what checking leaves behind.

text:
India has quietly frozen Starlink. It issued the license nearly a year ago, then let the final security clearance sit, and the whole satellite-comms sector has slowed with it. This is not a compliance dispute. New Delhi is asking a question Starlink can't really answer: given its US ownership and global network, how can it promise to follow Indian rules when Washington wants the opposite?

What spooked them is concrete. Starlink terminals were used in the Iran war even though it holds no license in Iran. India watched a sovereign state fail to switch off a network running over its own territory, and asked who is next.

Notice the tell. Jio and Bharti get an easier ride because their satellite partners are European, not a US-controlled operator. The worry isn't the satellites, it's whose hand is on the switch. And it lands days before SpaceX's IPO at a $1.75tn valuation, with Starlink as the main revenue engine, a reminder that the global rollout is far from uniform: shut out of China, and now stuck in India too.

Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

New Delhi, 16 June 2026.

My neighbor installed a security camera that could see straight into my bedroom, and when I asked him to move it, he refused. So I mounted a mirror facing his camera and took him to court. He thought I was the problem until the judge saw the footage.

My neighbor, Warren, moved in two years ago. He’s in his fifties, loud, opinionated, and always looking for something to complain about. We’ve never been friends, but we’ve always managed to keep things civil.

That changed last spring when he installed a large white security camera on a pole near our shared fence.

At first, I didn’t think much of it. I assumed it was monitoring his driveway. But one evening, while I was sitting in my backyard, I noticed the camera’s red light blinking.

I moved to the other side of the patio.

The camera followed me.

I walked toward my garden.

It followed me again.

That’s when I realized something was seriously wrong.

I checked the camera’s position from the other side of the fence and discovered it had a clear view of my entire backyard, including my patio, hot tub, garden, and, worst of all, my second-floor bedroom window.

text:
The following morning, I went to speak with Warren.

Me: Warren, I noticed your new camera is pointing directly into my backyard. It can even see inside my bedroom.

Warren: It’s a security camera. I’m allowed to have security cameras on my property.

Me: I’m not asking you to remove it. I’m asking you to adjust the angle so it doesn’t record my private space.

Warren: No. I installed it for a reason, and I’m not changing anything.

Me: You understand that someone could be watching my bedroom through that camera?

Warren: Then close your curtains.

I honestly couldn’t believe what I was hearing.

I went home and wrote him a formal letter explaining my concerns. I asked him to reposition the camera within seven days.

He ignored it.

I contacted the HOA, hoping they would intervene, but their response was that security cameras were a private matter between neighbors.

I even called the police.

An officer came out, looked at the camera, and explained that the situation might require a civil complaint unless there was evidence of criminal surveillance or another specific violation.

Warren apparently took that as permission to continue.

A few days later, he actually bragged to another neighbor that nobody could tell him what to do on his own property.

That’s when I decided to stop asking nicely.

I bought a large outdoor mirror and mounted it on my side of the fence at an angle that reflected directly toward his camera.

Suddenly, his precious security camera was getting a beautiful reflection of itself.

A few hours later, Warren came storming over.

Warren: What on earth is that thing?

Me: A mirror.

text:
Last night IFF, @SFLCin and @geoblockedindia received a legal notice said to be issued purportedly on behalf of the RSS. It’s hard to believe this comes from an organisation that has had a century to practise its paperwork and hence this may even be a weird prank! This notice asks us to stop criticising the Government’s blocking orders and stop documenting them. It also wants us to confirm in writing within seven days (seriously).

We can tell it’s an excellent teaching aid and here are seven lessons from it.

1) Say who you are: The notice names no advocate and gives no enrollment number. It is signed by an “Authorised Signatory” with no name. Replies go to a free Proton Mail ID, and the “office” is a residential flat in outer Delhi. A notice that can’t tell you who sent it is less a legal document than a weather event.

2) Have a grievance of your own: It never says how its client is harmed when we criticise a MeitY advisory. It complains on behalf of the Government’s blocking orders. The Union has no shortage of lawyers, and it hasn’t asked for volunteers.

3) Name the law: It threatens “appropriate legal action” under “the applicable provisions of law” and doesn’t cite a single section of any statute. A threat with no law, is literally an empty threat.

4) Don’t ask people to give up a fundamental right within seven days: The first demand is that we stop “publicly opposing” government directions. In Shreya Singhal (2015), the Supreme Court held that discussion and advocacy of a cause, however unpopular, sit at the heart of Article 19(1)(a). Opposing an order is how its legality gets tested. That is the Constitution working as intended.

5) Check whether the courts asked for the thing you want stopped” In Anuradha Bhasin (2020), the Supreme Court held that orders restricting fundamental rights must be made available so people can challenge them. The Reddit order is on the public Lumen Database because Reddit put it there. Reading a public database and saying what’s in it has a name. It’s called research.

6) Show us the spark and the powder keg: The notice says our work weakens national security measures, but it gives no instance, date or harm. In S. Rangarajan (1989), the Supreme Court held that the danger feared from speech can’t be remote, conjectural or far-fetched. It has to be like a spark in a powder keg. A post about a Lumen filing is not a spark.

7) Read it once more before you press send: The paragraphs run 1, then an empty 2 and 3, then 4. A PIN code wanders into the facts. The account it targets is on “Twitter”. 

Our reply is short. The notice is legally deficient because it makes no material allegation and cites no illegality. We will respectfully continue to advance constitutional rights, as we have done before. Notices like this rarely expect to win in court. They expect the recipient to get tired. We often are tired, but it has never changed what we do. Solidarity with @SFLCin and @geoblockedindia. 

If your post or account has been blocked in India, write to legal@internetfreedom.in.

text:
Statement : The removal of BitChat from the India App Store is unconstitutional. Section 69A permits the blocking of unlawful information, not of a messenger for working during internet shutdowns.

New Delhi, 3 October 2026

An Apple App Review notice published today by Jack Dorsey on X records that BitChat has been removed from the India App Store "per demand from the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology", issued under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, on the ground that the application "includes content that is illegal in India". The notice adds that BitChat's TestFlight builds are no longer available for testing in India. It does not identify the content said to be illegal or the ground under Section 69A invoked. The blocking order has not been published. The Internet Freedom Foundation condemns the order and calls for its immediate publication and withdrawal.

BitChat relays end-to-end encrypted messages between nearby phones over Bluetooth mesh. It has no servers and hosts no content of its own. What travels through it is the private speech of its users, so the claim that the application "includes" illegal content is incoherent. The State's actual objection stands recorded in the notices the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre issued on 23 July 2026 to GitHub, Google and Apple against BitChat, Briar and Bridgefy which stated that such applications work even during internet shutdowns and hamper lawful interception, attribution and traceability. Those notices, issued under Section 79(3)(b) were reportedly withdrawn after public disclosure. The same end has now been pursued through Section 69A. The objection is to capability of an application, not to content it transmits. A citizen's ability to speak to another citizen while the State has switched the internet off is not a ground of restriction under Section 69A or Article 19(2) of the Constitution.

Section 69A survived constitutional scrutiny in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) because of its safeguards which included the need for a reasoned, recorded order, committee review, and a hearing to the originator under Rule 8 of the Blocking Rules, 2009, which the Delhi High Court enforced in Tanul Thakur v. Union of India (2022). Further, Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) requires that orders restricting fundamental rights be published and adopt the least restrictive measure. However, it appears in this instance, each safeguard has been evaded. A secret order blocking an entire application, rather than any identified unlawful information, is the most restrictive and disproprotionate measure available. Further, the confidentiality claimed under Rule 16 cannot defeat the right to challenge an order, and the constitutionality of this blocking regime is itself pending consideration before the Supreme Court.

While removal from the App Store does not delete BitChat from phones, it stops new downloads and security updates, leaving existing users on unpatched versions, and it ends security testing in India through TestFlight. During the Jantar Mantar protests, when mobile internet was suspended and jammers were deployed, Bluetooth mesh messaging was a channel of last resort through which young people coordinated their safety. To our knowledge, Apple has removed BitChat on a government's demand in only one other country. This is in China, in April this year.

Our demands

1. MeitY must publish the blocking order, the ground invoked and the record of the committee's proceedings, and serve the developers with a copy and an opportunity of hearing.

2. The direction must be withdrawn. Any specific unlawful use must be met with targeted proceedings under due process, not the removal of a communications tool for everyone.

3. Apple must disclose the demand in its transparency reporting and notify its users in India, and must state whether parallel directions have been received in respect of other app stores.

4. The secrecy of the blocking regime must end. The Blocking Rules, 2009 should be amended to require publication of orders and notice to originators, without awaiting the outcome of the pending constitutional challenge.

The Internet Freedom Foundation will file applications under the Right to Information Act seeking a copy of the order, and stands ready to assist the developers and affected users in India.

I have my twitter back. 

It took me 6 days, a cyber police complaint and a legal notice to twitter to recover my account. 

If you got a DM from me last week asking you to vote for me for a podcast, that was not me. Please don't click it & If you already did, please change your password ASAP.

Here's what happened:

→I received a late night DM from a friend to vote on a podcast which redirected me to a a login page that looked right, and I typed in my password (classic)

→The attacker logged in and changed my 2FA within minutes & I was locked out of my account. (I still don't understand how my email and phone number were changed. Neither my email nor my phone was compromised.)

→Then he used account to DM followers a fake "vote for me" link. Each person who clicks becomes the next account sending it. That is how these spread.

What didn't work:

→ I filed X's hacked account form within the hour. Less than two hours later, the reply came: X could not verify me as the account owner. Their suggestion was to create a new account. Once 2FA is changed, the automated system treats the attacker as the real owner.

→ So I went to the Grievance Officer. Under the IT Rules, 2021, X must appoint a Resident Grievance Officer in India. He has no email address. X does not accept legal notices by email. 

The only options are a web form or post to their physical office.

Here's what worked:

→First, a cyber complaint on https://t.co/Uzds8BObDW (or call 1930).

→Second, a legal notice to the Grievance Officer. Under the IT Rules, impersonation complaints must be acted on within 24 hours.

→Third, the same notice sent by registered post, and to every X email address I could find.

The notice put X on record. It set out the ticket number, the phishing link, and the cyber complaint number. It showed proof of ownership: the registered email, the phone number, and the Premium subscription paid from my card. It ended with a clear ask and a deadline.

Six days after the hack, I was back in.

If this happens to you:
• Act within hours
• File X's hacked account form from your registered email and be persistent (this is important)
• File at https://t.co/Uzds8BObDW and keep the acknowledgement
• Notice to the Grievance Officer via the https://t.co/YkDfcMQwzE form and by post

text:
Delhi Police asks X to take down IFF's account and posts. IFF will challenge the notices in court unless they are withdrawn.

The Delhi Police has asked X to remove the Internet Freedom Foundation's account, six of its posts, the accounts of SFLC and @geoblockedindia, and posts by 16 other users, on the ground that they defame the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh. The posts document and comment on a legal notice sent in the RSS's name to IFF, SFLC and @geoblockedindia, which demanded that the three stop criticising and documenting government blocking orders. IFF received copies of the two police notices from X on the morning of 3 November 2026.
IFF calls on the Delhi Police to withdraw both notices. If they are not withdrawn, IFF will challenge them in court.

What has happened

On 29 October 2026 at 9:54 PM, IFF, SFLC and the operator of @geoblockedindia received a two-page "legal notice" said to be issued on behalf of the RSS. It asked the three to stop opposing the government's blocking directions, stop documenting restricted content, stop posting details of geo-blocked posts, and confirm in writing within seven days that they would comply. It was signed by an unnamed "Authorised Signatory". Several RSS office-bearers have since said on X that the notice is not authentic. IFF replied to the notice, wrote to the RSS at its official address asking whether it had authorised it, and published both the notice and its reply on 30 October.

On 31 October 2026 at 8:06 PM, the Special Commissioner of Police (Crime), Delhi Police, filed an "Illegal Content Report" with X (reference LD-321926). It listed two posts: IFF's post of 30 October on the notice, and SFLC post of the same day. The stated reason was that the posts are "defamatory towards the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh under Section 356 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023". The boxes for "safety/security", "defamation" and "other" were ticked. The fields for the nature of the court order and court order details were left empty. The desired action was "Remove/withhold content".

On 1 November 2026, a second notice arrived in the RSS's name. It said the matter had been handed to the Akhil Bharatiya Adhivakta Parishad, that complaints had been filed in several states, and that requests had been made to block IFF's X account and suspend the organisations. The Delhi Police had made its first request to X the previous evening. IFF did not know this until X told it on 3 November.

On 2 November 2026 at 8:51 AM, the Special Commissioner of Police (Crime) filed a second notice with X (reference LD-322956). It lists 40 URLs. Thirty-seven are posts. Three are the entire accounts of @internetfreedom, @SFLCin and @geoblockedindia. This time the boxes for "Hate speech", "defamation", "safety/security", "enforcement of court order" and "other" were all ticked. The court order fields were again left empty. The stated reason reads: "The posts constitute defamation and illegal content under Section 356 BNS. Under Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021, read with Section 79(3)(b) IT Act, lawful notices require action within 3 hours."

The 16 other users are @ProdctiveUseful, @PanjwaniManoj, @jidge_, @RatanSharda55, @baxiabhishek, @SchrdingersDbag, @ashleshbiradar, @seemay, @NasirHussainINC, @Being_creat_ive, @AjoyDharmavaram, @othlaw, @_ananyaaa, @AimPoojaind, @incorigibleBhai and @rraoind. Their posts, as far as IFF can tell, comment on the notice or on the notice about it.

X forwarded both notice to IFF on 3 November 2026, at 8:47 AM and 10:03 AM, saying it was doing so "in the interest of transparency" and that IFF may wish to seek legal counsel and challenge the request in court. X's emails do not say that it has acted on the requests. The Delhi Police has not written to IFF, and no court has been approached, as far as the reports disclose. SFLC and @geoblockedindia have separately reported notifications from X about requests from the Uttar Pradesh Police, the Telangana Police and the Delhi Police's Cyber Crime unit, one of them against the whole of the @geoblockedindia account.

IFF's position

IFF condemns this legal action. A police force has made itself the enforcement arm of a private legal notice whose authenticity the organisation it names has not confirmed, and whose demand was that three organisations stop documenting censorship. The notices would deliver exactly what the notice asked for as they would also remove the accounts of the three groups in India that keep public records of what is blocked, and of who ordered it.

The posts in question are about a legal notice sent to us. They quote it, criticise how it was drafted, and say that we will carry on with our work. A person who receives a threat is entitled to publish it and answer it and that is not defamation of the sender. 

In the three weeks before the first notice, IFF assisted 86 people whose accounts were suspended or whose posts were withheld in India. SFLC's Free Speech Tracker recorded about 268 content restrictions and 83 account restrictions in the first 29 days of October. @geoblockedindia publishes the orders behind such blocks when platforms disclose them. None of this is unlawful. Documenting censorship and challenging it in court is what the Constitution expects of citizens.
IFF will not delete the posts. If the Delhi Police does not withdraw the notices, we will challenge them in court.

Why the reports are unlawful

Defamation is not a police matter. Section 356 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 is a non-cognizable and bailable offence. Under Section 222 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, no court can take cognizance of it except on a complaint by the person aggrieved. 

Under Section 174 of the BNSS, the police cannot investigate a non-cognizable offence without an order of a Magistrate. The Special Commissioner of Police (Crime) is not the person aggrieved. The notices disclose no complaint by the RSS and no order of any Magistrate. Whether a statement is defamatory is for a court to decide after hearing its author, with the defences of truth, fair comment and good faith available to that author. 

In Subramanian Swamy v. Union of India, (2016) 7 SCC 221, the Supreme Court upheld criminal defamation on the strength of these safeguards. A police officer who asks a platform to remove speech as defamatory has decided the question himself, without a complainant, a court or a hearing.

The posts are protected comment. Exceptions 1 to 3 to Section 356(1) protect the truth published for the public good, opinion on the public conduct of public servants, and opinion on the conduct of any person touching a public question. The posts publish a notice that was sent to us and give our opinion of it. The RSS, if it sent the notice, chose to enter a public question. If it did not, the posts defame no one.

Further, Section 79(3)(b) and Rule 3(1)(d) do not permit this. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India, (2015) 5 SCC 1, the Supreme Court read down Section 79(3)(b) so that an intermediary acquires "actual knowledge" only through a court order, or a notification from the appropriate government or its agency that unlawful acts relatable to Article 19(2) are being committed. The court said that it would be difficult for intermediaries to judge the legitimacy of the millions of requests they receive, and that the burden must not be placed on them. Rule 3(1)(d), as amended in November 2025 and February 2026, now requires the intimation to come from an officer not below the rank of Joint Secretary or Deputy Inspector General, to be reasoned, and to specify the legal basis and the nature of the unlawful act, subject to a monthly review by a Secretary-level officer. The three-hour window the notice invokes applies to a lawful order that meets these conditions. A web form that ticks "hate speech" and "enforcement of court order" while leaving the court order fields blank, and that gives one sentence of reasons for 40 URLs, is not such an order.

The notices by the Delhi Police are disproportionate. They seek to remove three accounts in their entirety, with years of posts, over six, four and eleven posts respectively. They sweep in 16 third parties whose only connection is that they commented on a public controversy. In Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637, the Supreme Court held that any restriction on speech must be necessary, proportionate and the least restrictive measure available, and that orders restricting speech must be published and reasoned. Removing an organisation's entire account for criticising a legal notice fails each of these tests.

The effect is to silence documentation of censorship and providing legal aid to Indian internet users. The accounts named are those that record blocking orders in India. The notice asked them to stop. A takedown request that accomplishes the demand of an anonymous private notice is not law enforcement. It is the use of state power for a private end, which Article 14 forbids.

Our demands

1. To the Delhi Police: Withdraw reports LD-321926 and LD-322956 and confirm the withdrawal in writing to X and to IFF. 

2. To the Delhi Police: Disclose the complaint on which the Special Commissioner of Police (Crime) acted, the authority under which the reports were filed, and whether any order of a Magistrate under Section 174 BNSS exists. Disclose every request made to any platform in this matter, including those made by the Cyber Crime unit against @geoblockedindia.

3. To X: Do not act on the reports. If any content is withheld in India, tell the affected user before acting, give them the full request, and name the legal basis. Publish both reports to the Lumen database, as the reporting form itself contemplates.

4. To the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology and the Ministry of Home Affairs: Have the Secretary-level review required by Rule 3(1)(d) examine these intimations, and tell police forces that Rule 3(1)(d) is not a remedy for defamation, which the law reserves to the person aggrieved and to the courts.

5. To the RSS: State publicly whether it authorised either notice or any complaint to the police. If it did not, say so to the Delhi Police.

If the notices are not withdrawn, IFF will challenge them in court. We will continue to document blocking orders, to publish them, and to provide legal assistance to anyone whose account or post is withheld in India. Nothing in these notices changes that.

MeitY's advisory to Meta directs the suppression of protest reporting on Instagram and Facebook. It must be withdrawn.

19 Oct 2026

On 10 October 2026, the Cyber Laws Division of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology issued an advisory to Meta Platforms bearing File No. 6(2)/2026-Cyberlaws. It was not published on the MEITY website and first HT and then PTI reported it on 18 October. Any such advisory is not a legal order and MEITY is not legally empowered to issue them on the basis of any statutory provision. This advisory followed, by two days, an advisory of 8 October to all social media intermediaries calling for "enhanced diligence" over content on "ongoing public events", asking platforms to "label or add context" to misleading content and to "give priority to complaints from authorised Government agencies".  IFF called for the withdrawal of that advisory on 9 October. The Meta advisory was issued on the day the Delhi Police detained protesters and journalists at the demonstrations called over the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls.

The advisory states that content relating to "public-order and law and order situations" is being "prominently displayed and recommended" on Meta's platforms and, "when presented without adequate context or disproportionately amplified", "may contribute to public confusion, apprehension and disturbance of public order and social tranquillity". It singles out "unverified or misleading claims regarding the imposition of emergency, restrictions, police action or other official measures". Further, Meta is advised to review its "recommendation and content ranking mechanisms", to ensure its systems "do not result in disproportionate exposure of users to a single or limited set of narratives", and to furnish "information or assistance" to law enforcement, "with immediate effect". PTI reports that the Ministry acted on inputs from "agencies" that Meta's platforms were not promoting all "narratives" equally.

This advisory matches restrictions on META platforms related to protest content and reporting in the same timline. On 10 October, the Instagram account of Molitics India was withheld in India. On 11 October, a Mathrubhumi English reel showing a woman clinging to a pole as police officers attempted to detain her was restricted citing, "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement", and a video report by Observer Post Hindi was restricted on Facebook by what Meta called an "automated system" acting under the IT Rules, 2021. On 12 October, the Instagram account of journalist Shubhangi Das Gupta was restricted in India for alleged non-compliance with "local IT Rules". On 13 October, the account of Journo Mirror (about five lakh followers) was withheld. The account of Fridays For Future India has since been withheld without any stated reason. Meta's notices to these users do not disclose what is unlawful about the content. 

As per notices shared by us by those who have been censored by META, they take two forms: 

1. "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement under Section 79(3)(b)", and, 

2. "through an automated system implemented pursuant to legal requirements under India's Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules". 

Neither names the issuing agency, the order, the provision of law or offence the content is said to disclose, or the URL complained of. We know due to litigation that the first notice related to a Sahyog order issued by a Law Enforcement Agency (LEA), while the second one is without any legal order. At the same time, several users received no communication at all. Instagram used the same "automated system" notice against Anjali Priya, Varnika Dhawan and Sachin Gupta after the July protests, and against cartoonist Satish Acharya, who lost nine cartoons and then his account between February and September 2026. 

In April 2026, The Hindu reported that Meta automatically restricts government and police flagged content in India at scale, and seeks a separate government direction before restoring content later found to be legally unsupported. IFF objected to Meta on 4 May 2026. IFF condemns the advisory of 10 October and the restrictions imposed in its wake. An executive communication that instructs a platform to suppress "unverified" claims about "police action" and to correct a "limited set of narratives", issued on the day of a police crackdown and kept from the public, is a censorship directive in all but name.  It makes the State the editor of what Indians may see of a protest against the State. IFF calls upon MeitY to withdraw it and upon Meta to disclose what it has done under it.

Our demands

1. MeitY must withdraw the advisories of 8 and 10 October 2026 forthwith and publish them.

2. MeitY must abandon proposed Rule 3(4) and restrict content only by reasoned, published orders under Section 69A or notices compliant with Rule 3(1)(d).

3. Meta must disclose every takedown, account restriction and act of downranking carried out under the advisories, and its compliance report to the Ministry.

4. Meta must restore the accounts and posts of journalists, outlets and creators restricted since 8 October 2026 unless it holds a valid legal order, and must furnish that order to the person affected.

5. Meta must suspend the automated restriction of content in India and disclose on what inputs its "automated system" acts.

Any person whose account or content has been withheld in India since 8 October 2026 may write to IFF at legal@internetfreedom.in. IFF is providing assistance pro bono.

Bhai aur beheno, agar aap bhi Binance P2P trading karte ho aur suddenly bank account freeze ho gaya hai toh pareshan mat ho. Yeh bahut common problem hai India mein. Innocent log bhi fas jaate hain jab kisi buyer/seller ka paisa kisi fraud case se link hota hai.

Yeh steps follow karo - 

1️⃣ Sabse Pehle Bank Branch Jaao  
   - Freeze ka exact reason, Cyber Crime complaint number, IO naam aur Police Station details lo.  
   - Written notice maang lo.

2️⃣ Saare Proofs Collect Karo (Bahut Important)  
   - Binance P2P complete order history (screenshots)  
   - Buyer/Seller ke saath chat  
   - Payment proof (UPI, bank transfer screenshot)  
   - Bank statement jisme transaction dikhe  
   - Aadhaar, PAN, Binance account details

3️⃣ Binance Support ko turant contact karo  
   - App mein Help section → Submit ticket  
   - Order ID aur proofs attach karo. Woh counterparty ko investigate kar sakte hain.

4️⃣ Cyber Cell mein Representation Daalo  
   - Local Cyber Police Station ya online portal pe jaao.  
   - Detailed application likho ki transaction genuine tha Binance P2P pe hua.  
   - Saare proofs attach karo.  
   - Lawyer (Cyber crime specialist) ki madad le lo - yeh bahut kaam aata hai.

5️⃣ Follow-up karte raho  
   - Har 7-10 din mein bank aur cyber cell ko call/email karo.  
   - Partial release ke liye request kar sakte ho.

Extra Tips jo future mein bacha sakte hain:
• P2P ke liye alag dedicated bank account use karo (savings account mat use karo)
• Sirf verified buyers/sellers ke saath trade karo

The Kerala Government has revealed that it ordered the takedown of 15,627 posts, news cards, photographs and video links from social media platforms in the six months since it assumed office in May 2026. The figures were shared by Home Minister Ramesh Chennithala in a written reply to a question raised by Xavier Chittilappilly, MLA, in the Kerala Legislative Assembly.

The disclosure comes amid controversy over the government's role in restricting online content. In August 2026, several media organisations reported instances of their content being taken down. At the time, Chief Minister V. D. Satheesan stated at a press conference that his government had not issued any instructions to Meta to block content. Subsequent media reports suggested that some of these restrictions were caused by technical glitches.

However, the government's involvement in issuing blocking orders came to light during cases filed before the Kerala High Court by NOCAP, an independent digital media organisation, and the Kerala Independent Farmers Association (KIFA), after their Facebook pages were blocked. In both cases, the High Court ordered the restoration of the pages, observing that objections to specific posts or comments did not justify blocking an entire social media account.

These cases sparked a political controversy, with the Opposition accusing the Congress-led government of using police and administrative authorities to restrict online criticism. Questions were subsequently raised in the Legislative Assembly, leading to the disclosure of the number of takedown directions issued by the government.

The Delhi High Court has issued notice on a constitutional challenge to the automated filter which Meta operates on Instagram and Facebook in India, and to Rule 4(4) of the IT Rules, 2021. On 19 November 2026, the Court issued notice to the Union of India and to Meta on a writ petition filed by Live Law Media Private Limited and its Director, Sindhu T.P. IFF is supporting LiveLaw in this challenge. (1/10)
Read More: https://t.co/s5ichxKjPu

The petition contends that Rule 4(4) exceeds the powers conferred by the IT Act, creates a blocking regime outside Section 69A, and operates as a prior restraint on the press. A publisher whose report is suppressed by automated tools receives no notice, no reasons and no hearing. The grievance route offers little, since 54,918 appeals were pending before the Grievance Appellate Committee on 2 November 2026. (9/10)

The Court has granted the respondents four weeks to file their counter-affidavits and has listed the matter on 18 January 2027. A Department of Telecommunications report found in October 2025 that the jammers and call blocking towers at Bengaluru Central Prison disrupt mobile networks up to 700 metres away, in apparent violation of government guidelines. More than a year later, residents of Parappana Agrahara still have no reliable mobile or Wi-Fi service at home. (1/7)
Read More: https://t.co/WzoMY5qWpK

This is not an isolated incident. Residents near prisons in Mangaluru, Kalaburagi, Ballari, Belagavi, Amritsar, Patiala, Delhi and Kerala have reported similar disruptions. Yet India has no published standard on how far a prison jammer’s signal may reach. The only guidelines the WMO supplied apply to “VIP movement and Examination halls”. The UK and the US have written rules to limit interference outside prisons. (6/7)

We have written to DoT, the WMO, the MHA, TRAI and the Government of Karnataka. We have asked that the WMO’s corrections be carried out within 30 days and independently verified, and that a binding national standard for prison jammers be framed. We are also filing RTI applications and will assist the resident before the KSHRC. If you live near a prison and have lost mobile or Wi-Fi service, write to us at legal@internetfreedom.in. (7/7)
